prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The Devil’s tour of hell did not include a factory line where molten lead spilled into mouths held wide, no electric drill spiraling screws into hands and feet, nor giant pliers to lower you into simmering vats. Instead, a circle of light opened on your stuffed armchair, whose chintz orchids did not boil and change, and the Devil adjusted your new spiked antennae almost delicately, with claws curled and lacquered black, before he spread his leather wings to leap into the acid-green sky. So your head became a tv hull, a gargoyle mirror. Your doppelganger sloppy at the mouth and swollen at the joints enacted your days in sinuous slow motion, your lines delivered with a mocking sneer. Sometimes the frame froze, reversed, began again: the red eyes of a friend you cursed, your girl child cowered behind the drapes, parents alive again and puzzled by this new form. That’s why you clawed your way back to this life.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, Devil, Instead

outputs.L1:
The Devil’s tour of hell included no factory line where molten lead spilled into mouths held wide, no electric drill spiraling screws into hands and feet, nor giant pliers lowering you into simmering vats. Instead, a circle of light opened upon your stuffed armchair, whose chintz orchids neither boiled nor changed, and the Devil adjusted your new spiked antennae almost delicately, his claws curled and lacquered black, before spreading his leather wings and leaping into the acid-green sky.

And so your head became a TV hull, a gargoyle mirror. Your doppelgänger, sloppy at the mouth and swollen at the joints, enacted your days in sinuous slow motion, delivering your lines with a mocking sneer. Sometimes the frame froze, reversed, and began again: the red eyes of a friend you cursed; your girl child cowering behind the drapes; your parents alive again, puzzled by this new form. That is why you clawed your way back to this life.
outputs.L2:
The Devil’s guided journey through the underworld featured no assembly line pouring liquid lead into forced-open mouths, no powered drill driving screws through palms and soles, and no enormous pincers dipping bodies into bubbling tanks. What appeared instead was a bright ring upon your overstuffed chair, while the orchids printed on its chintz remained unchanged and cool. With an almost gentle touch, the Devil positioned your newly sprouted, thorny antennae, his black-lacquered talons curved inward. Then he unfurled leathery wings and launched himself into the corrosive green heavens.

Your skull was transformed into the casing of a television, a grotesque reflective screen. Inside it, a duplicate of you—drooling, joints distended—performed your life with fluid, unnatural slowness, reciting your words through a derisive curl of the lips. At moments, the image stopped, ran backward, and started over: a companion you had condemned staring with crimson eyes; your young daughter shrinking behind the curtains; your dead parents restored, bewildered by what you had become. This was the reason you fought and scraped your way back into the living world.
outputs.L3:
Hell is portrayed not as a place of physical torture, but as a state of inescapable self-confrontation. The speaker is trapped in a familiar armchair and forced to watch the events of their own life unfold before them. The Devil transforms the speaker’s head into a television-like mirror, its screen reflecting a grotesque double. This doppelganger reenacts the speaker’s sinful actions in exaggerated, mocking slow motion, turning every wrongdoing into a cruel spectacle.

The most painful memories recur endlessly: scenes involving a cursed friend, a frightened daughter, and bewildered parents play, rewind, and begin again. Each repetition intensifies the speaker’s guilt and forces them to witness the suffering they have caused. Ultimately, this psychological torment proves more unbearable than physical pain. Desperate to escape the relentless confrontation with their past, the speaker claws their way back toward life.
outputs.L4:
Hell, in the passage, is not a place of flames, chains, or physical torture. Instead, it is a state of relentless psychological suffering. The condemned self is represented through surreal imagery as a figure with a television for a head, trapped before the screen and forced to watch the worst moments of the past replay again and again. Every act of cruelty, every betrayal, and every humiliating failure becomes part of an inescapable broadcast. There is no way to look away, change the channel, or soften what happened.

The most painful scenes are not those in which the central figure suffered, but those that reveal the suffering inflicted on loved ones. Words once spoken carelessly now appear brutal; selfish actions are shown through the eyes of the people they wounded. Shame intensifies as the condemned person finally recognizes the full consequences of their behavior. Hell is therefore presented as perfect self-knowledge: a place where excuses disappear and the truth can no longer be avoided.

This realization becomes more unbearable than any physical punishment. Overwhelmed by remorse, the figure resists condemnation and begins to claw a way back toward life. The return is desperate rather than triumphant, driven by the need to change what can still be changed and to seek forgiveness for what cannot be undone.

Ultimately, the passage suggests that remorse can be both punishment and salvation. Honest self-recognition causes immense pain, but it also creates the possibility of redemption. By confronting past cruelty instead of denying it, the condemned self discovers a reason to return, take responsibility, and become someone different.
outputs.L5:
### The Devil Instead

At the crossroads, Mara expected an angel.

She had walked three days through rain, carrying one question like a stone inside her chest: *How can I change my life?*

But when midnight came, the devil appeared instead.

He wore no horns. He carried no fire. He looked tired, almost ordinary, and held out a small mirror.

“Is this the price?” Mara asked.

“No,” he said. “The price is looking.”

In the mirror, she saw every excuse she had polished into truth, every kindness postponed, every dream abandoned because fear had spoken first.

She tried to turn away.

“You wanted an angel,” the devil said, “because you hoped to be rescued.”

“And what do you offer?”

“Nothing.”

Mara looked again. This time, beyond the fear, she saw a road she had always been free to take.

By dawn, the devil was gone.

Mara walked home—not saved, not forgiven, but finally responsible for herself.

Sometimes grace arrives with wings.

Sometimes the devil comes instead.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in the second person about the Devil showing someone a personalized hell that forces them to watch their past sins replayed on a television-like head.
counterfactuals.output:
The Devil meets you in a room wallpapered with your own fingerprints.

He is smaller than rumor. He wears a red suit stitched from emergency exits, and where his face should be, an old television flickers—glass bowed outward, silver knobs clicking by themselves. Two antennae rise like the horns of an insect praying for rain.

“Nothing here is eternal,” he tells you, “except the reruns.”

Then his screen brightens.

You see the afternoon you lied beneath a yellow ceiling. Your mouth moves before you remember the words; nevertheless, the words remember you. They crawl from the speaker in a nest of static. Each syllable has tiny hands.

You try to turn away, but the room turns with you.

Click.

Now the screen shows the door you did not open. On the other side, someone is weeping in the soft, patient manner of snow. You watch yourself stand in the hallway, holding your breath as if silence were innocence.

Click.

A garden appears. Every flower has the face of someone you wounded, though some wounds were only pinpricks, though some were given carelessly, though some you called necessary. Their petals open and close around your name.

“Commercial break?” you ask.

The Devil smiles through a burst of static.

There are no advertisements, only desires you traded yourself for: a table set with applause, a bed filled with mirrors, a golden key that unlocks no door but makes a beautiful sound in the pocket.

You reach for the dial on his cheek.

It comes off in your hand like a black tooth.

The channels continue changing.

You see betrayals too small for history. Cups left unwashed. Calls unanswered. The insect crushed under your heel because the day had made you feel powerless. Each act enlarged to cathedral size, each omission given weather. Your past does not accuse you. It simply occurs, again and again, with the unbearable calm of a moon rising over a graveyard.

At last you understand the punishment: not fire, not hooks, not the red machinery turning below the floor.

It is that you must watch without editing.

You must sit beside the Devil while his television head hums with your vanished life. You must see every version of yourself believing it was the final version. You must hear the laughter after you left the room, the silence after you spoke, the long echo of what you could have done.

And worst of all, in the blue light, the Devil takes your hand gently.

As if he forgives you.

As if he knows you never will.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single paragraph of literary horror in which hell is not physical torture but an endless, distorted reenactment of the protagonist’s cruelty toward friends, family, and a frightened daughter.
counterfactuals.output: Hell had no fire, only rooms he recognized: the kitchen where his mother’s hands trembled around a chipped cup, the hallway where his oldest friend waited for an apology that never came, the darkened bedroom where his daughter, small in her moon-patterned pajamas, asked why he was shouting and whether he still loved her. In each room he entered wearing the face of the person he had wounded, while something else—something with his voice, his posture, his patient little sneer—performed his cruelties exactly as he remembered them and worse than he remembered them, stretching every silence into years, every insult into a verdict, every slammed door into the sound of a world ending. He felt his mother swallow her grief, felt his friend’s hope rot by degrees, felt his daughter’s fear make a permanent home beneath her ribs; and when at last he broke, sobbing apologies through borrowed mouths, the rooms reset with a soft domestic click. The cup was whole again. The friend stood waiting. His daughter looked up. And from somewhere just behind his eyes, he heard himself begin.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a vivid, experimental flash-fiction passage explaining why a damned soul clawed its way back to life. Include the Devil, an armchair with chintz orchids, an acid-green sky, and grotesque television imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
The Devil kept an armchair upholstered in chintz orchids at the mouth of Hell.

This was the first insult.

The second was the television.

It had no cabinet, no cord, no glass—only a fleshy screen stretched between antlers. It showed the living world in obscene close-up: mouths chewing birthday cake; thumbs worrying loose teeth; surgeons lifting a blue infant into light. Sometimes the channels changed by themselves. Weather. War. A game show whose contestants had deer legs and human mothers. A children’s cartoon in which a smiling sun peeled off its own face.

Above everything hung an acid-green sky, bright as poison, with black stars drifting through it like burnt crumbs.

The damned soul had forgotten its name. The Devil called it Pet.

“Sit,” said the Devil, patting the orchid chair.

Pet sat.

For nine hundred years—or one long afternoon—the television broadcast everything Pet had ruined. A father waiting beside a silent phone. A dog nosing an empty coat. A woman at a kitchen table, stirring cold coffee with a pregnancy test.

Pet watched without eyelids.

“Regret,” the Devil explained, “is the only program we get.”

Then the picture jumped.

Static swarmed. The antlers trembled. For one impossible second the screen showed not the past but now: a hospital room, fluorescent and rain-streaked. On a bed lay Pet’s former body, recently dredged from a river, tagged, refrigerated, declared. Beside it stood the woman from the kitchen, older by grief but still holding the positive test.

She placed Pet’s dead hand against the small, hard moon of her belly.

“There,” she whispered. “That’s your father.”

Inside the green sky of Hell, something cracked.

Not hope. Hope is too clean.

It was shame with a pulse in it.

Pet sprang from the orchid chair. The Devil laughed, because the dead are always funniest when they run. Pet ran anyway—through barbed choirs, through lakes that remembered every drowning, through corridors wallpapered with its own excuses. When the ground closed, Pet dug. When its fingers wore away, it clawed with wristbones. When the wristbones splintered, it bit upward with the black stumps of its teeth.

“Why?” the Devil called after it. “You’ll only fail them again.”

Yes, thought Pet.

That was why.

Not to become good. Not to be forgiven. Not even to stay alive.

Only to arrive before the child learned the shape of an absence.

In the morgue, the corpse arched.

River water burst from its lungs. The tag snapped from its toe. Machines screamed awake, painting the walls with grotesque blue organs, dancing skeletons, a weather map of impossible storms.

Far below, the Devil settled into the chintz orchids and changed the channel.

Above, under an ordinary gray sky, the damned soul opened its eyes and asked—hoarsely, terribly—for its name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a darkly poetic scene that subverts traditional images of infernal punishment: instead of drills, molten lead, or boiling vats, the condemned person must confront a monstrous doppelganger replaying their worst memories.
counterfactuals.output:
There were no drills in hell.

No iron teeth whining toward the skull, no ladles of molten lead, no black cauldrons where bodies turned slowly in their own screams. The condemned had prepared himself for these. He had imagined pain as a kind of weather—fire descending, metal entering, flesh becoming briefly important before it vanished.

Instead, they led him into a room with two chairs.

The walls were the color of old bone. Between the chairs stood a small wooden table, and on it, a glass of water. The water trembled though nothing moved.

“Sit,” said the keeper.

Across from him sat a thing wearing his face.

Not his face as it had been at death, but every face he had ever owned badly stitched together: the soft mouth of childhood, the proud jaw of youth, the pinched eyes of old age. Its skin shifted with each breath. Beneath it, other expressions pressed outward, as if drowned people were trapped under ice.

The keeper closed the door.

The doppelganger smiled.

It began with his mother.

The room loosened. The bone-colored walls became a kitchen at dusk. Rain worried the windows. A pot hissed on the stove, and his mother stood with her back to him, shoulders bowed beneath a grief he had mistaken for weakness.

He heard himself at seventeen.

*I wish you were dead.*

He remembered saying it. He had always remembered the anger, bright and righteous. He had forgotten the way she set down the spoon so carefully. He had forgotten her hand closing around the edge of the counter. He had forgotten that she did not turn around.

The creature across from him spoke in her voice.

“Say it again.”

“No.”

Its mouth widened.

The memory began again.

Rain. Steam. Bent shoulders.

*I wish you were dead.*

Again.

Again.

Each time, some new detail surfaced: the burn scar on her wrist; the cheap blue dress; the bowl she had set out for him before the argument began. Hell, he discovered, was not repetition.

It was improved accuracy.

He lunged across the table, but the kitchen vanished, and his hands closed on empty air.

Now there was a roadside in winter. A man lay beside an overturned bicycle, one trouser leg dark with blood. The condemned watched his younger self slow the car, meet the injured man’s eyes, and drive on.

“I was afraid,” he whispered.

The doppelganger wore the cyclist’s face now, though his own features moved beneath it like worms under cloth.

“You were late,” it corrected.

The scene replayed. Headlights swept over the fallen bicycle. A hand lifted weakly from the snow.

This time the condemned heard the radio in his car. A cheerful song. He had sung along three miles later.

“No,” he said.

Again.

The hand in the snow.

The song.

His own voice joining the chorus.

The glass of water remained on the table through every memory, impossible and untouched. He reached for it once. The doppelganger reached too, mirroring him, and in the water he saw not his reflection but a procession: his daughter waiting at a school gate; his brother reading the letter he had forged; his wife sitting awake beside a cold lamp, knowing before she knew.

Every cruelty he had buried returned without spectacle. No flames crowned them. No demons applauded. The room simply gave each wound back its original temperature.

At last he understood why there were two chairs.

One was for the man who had done these things.

The other was for the man who had spent a lifetime insisting he had not.

Across from him, the monster swelled, fed by every excuse. Its limbs bent beneath the weight of borrowed faces. His mother’s mouth opened in its chest. The cyclist’s hand protruded from its throat. His daughter’s eyes blinked from its palms.

He stared at it, horrified.

“What are you?” he asked.

The creature leaned close. Its breath smelled of rain, snow, hospital corridors, and all the rooms he had left without looking back.

Then it answered in his own voice:

“I am what happened after you forgave yourself.”

The door did not open.

The memories began again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: In lush, unsettling language and second-person perspective, describe a tour of hell where the Devil delicately fits the narrator with spiked antennae and turns their head into a screen that loops scenes of the people they harmed.
counterfactuals.output:
The Devil receives you in a garden that has learned to bloom without light.

Black lilies unfasten beneath your feet. Their petals are soft as tongues, and from each chalice rises the faint perfume of a room you once left in anger. The path winds downward through orchards hung with glass fruit. Inside every pear, every pomegranate, a small heart knocks patiently against the rind.

“Your tour,” the Devil says, “is also your fitting.”

He speaks with the courtesy of a tailor. His hands are pale, immaculate, almost tender. He seats you before a mirror framed in vertebrae and lifts two slender antennae from a velvet case. They are beautiful things—silver, jointed, jeweled with backward-facing spikes.

You try to ask what they receive.

“Only what you transmitted,” he says.

He parts your hair and presses the first antenna into your skull. Each barb enters with a tiny, courteous click. The second follows. Pain blossoms in exquisite filaments, branching behind your eyes until you can feel distant rooms tuning themselves to you: a kitchen after midnight, an office stairwell, a child’s bedroom, the rain-bright shoulder of a road.

Then the Devil cups your face.

His thumbs smooth away your features as if wiping breath from glass. Your mouth closes first, sealed beneath a cool, luminous surface. Your nose sinks soundlessly. Your eyes flatten into brightness. Where your head had been, a screen hums to life.

It begins with the people you harmed.

Not the grand injuries you rehearsed excuses for, but the smaller ones: the friend watching your message go unanswered; the stranger carrying your contempt home like a stain; the lover learning to apologize for needing warmth. Each scene loops. Each flinch returns. Each silence ripens again from its beginning.

You cannot look away. You have become the looking.

Along the corridors of Hell, doors open. The dead gather before your flickering face. Some recognize themselves. Some do not. The antennae quiver, catching every buried consequence, every echo you never stayed to hear. Their spikes hold the signal in place.

The Devil adjusts one by a fraction.

“There,” he murmurs. “Perfect reception.”

Then he wheels you onward through the flowering dark, while your bright new head plays the same sorrows without end, and all Hell pauses to watch.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
